primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Alveolar hyperventilation lowers arterial carbon dioxide, decreasing carbonic acid and raising blood pH.
vignette: A 23-year-old woman becomes intensely anxious before a procedure and begins breathing rapidly. She develops perioral tingling and lightheadedness. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.52 and PaCO2 27 mm Hg.
lead: Which primary acid-base disturbance is present?
distractors: Mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory acidosis
distractor_notes: Respiratory acidosis requires carbon dioxide retention with acidemia, not hypocapnia with alkalemia.
Metabolic acidosis has a primary reduction in bicarbonate and usually compensatory hyperventilation.
Metabolic alkalosis is driven primarily by elevated bicarbonate rather than reduced PaCO2 from hyperventilation.
A mixed acidosis would lower rather than raise pH.
key_expl: Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 and produces primary respiratory alkalosis.
objective: Identify respiratory alkalosis from alkalemia with primary hypocapnia after hyperventilation.

sources.title: Respiratory alkalosis
sources.support: MedlinePlus defines respiratory alkalosis as low blood carbon dioxide from excessive breathing and lists anxiety/hyperventilation as common causes.

sources.title: Alkalosis
sources.support: MedlinePlus explains that decreased carbon dioxide makes body fluids alkaline and describes respiratory alkalosis from overbreathing.

sources.title: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) Test
sources.support: MedlinePlus gives typical ABG reference ranges including arterial pH 7.35–7.45 and PaCO2 35–45 mmHg, confirming that pH 7.52 is alkalemic and PaCO2 27 mmHg is low.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Persistent carbon dioxide retention causes chronic respiratory acidosis; renal compensation increases bicarbonate retention/generation, partially restoring blood pH.
vignette: A 68-year-old man with long-standing severe COPD has an arterial blood gas of pH 7.36, PaCO2 60 mm Hg, and HCO3− 33 mEq/L. He is clinically stable.
lead: Which physiologic adaptation best explains the near-normal pH?
distractors: Marked reduction in hydrogen ion secretion
Hyperventilation that lowers PaCO2 below normal
distractor_notes: Bicarbonate loss would worsen acidosis rather than compensate for it.
Reduced renal hydrogen secretion would impair acid excretion and worsen acidemia.
The measured PaCO2 remains high, so pulmonary overcompensation is not occurring.
Gastric acid loss causes metabolic alkalosis and is not the chronic renal response to hypercapnia.
key_expl: In chronic respiratory acidosis, the kidneys raise body bicarbonate to buffer persistent CO2 retention and move pH toward normal.
objective: Explain renal compensation for chronic hypercapnic respiratory acidosis.
clues: high PaCO2 with elevated HCO3− and near-normal pH

sources.title: Respiratory acidosis
sources.support: MedlinePlus states that chronic respiratory acidosis leads the kidneys to increase bicarbonate and other body chemicals that help restore acid-base balance.

sources.title: Acidosis
sources.support: MedlinePlus explains respiratory acidosis as carbon dioxide accumulation from inadequate ventilation and the roles of lungs and kidneys in acid-base balance.

sources.title: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) Test
sources.support: MedlinePlus gives typical ABG reference ranges for pH, PaCO2, and bicarbonate, supporting interpretation of the elevated PaCO2 and bicarbonate with near-normal pH in this chronic compensated respiratory acidosis vignette.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Repeated airway infection and inflammation damage the bronchi, causing permanent abnormal widening of the large airways and chronic cough with large amounts of sputum.
vignette: A 45-year-old woman has years of daily productive cough with large amounts of sputum and recurrent respiratory infections. CT shows permanently dilated large airways.
lead: Which structural change best defines this disorder?
correct: Permanent widening of damaged large airways
distractors: Diffuse destruction of alveolar septa only
Uniform interstitial collagen deposition without airway dilation
Acute filling of alveoli with protein-rich edema
distractor_notes: Reversible bronchoconstriction is characteristic of asthma and does not produce permanent bronchial dilation.
Alveolar septal destruction defines emphysema rather than bronchiectasis.
Interstitial fibrosis primarily affects lung interstitium and compliance.
Protein-rich alveolar edema is a feature of acute lung injury rather than chronic dilated bronchi.
key_expl: Bronchiectasis is defined by permanent widening of damaged large airways, often in the setting of recurrent airway infection or inflammation.
objective: Link chronic purulent sputum and recurrent infections to permanent bronchial dilation.
clues: chronic cough with large amounts of sputum
CT with permanently dilated large airways

sources.title: Bronchiectasis
sources.support: MedlinePlus defines bronchiectasis as damage that causes large airways to become permanently wider and associates it with recurrent infection/inflammation.

sources.title: Bronchial Disorders
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes bronchiectasis as airway damage causing bronchi to widen, become flabby, and scarred.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Defects in motile ciliary proteins such as axonemal dynein impair coordinated ciliary beating, reducing mucociliary clearance and disrupting left-right embryonic patterning.
vignette: A 16-year-old boy has chronic sinusitis, recurrent otitis media, bronchiectasis, and situs inversus. Nasal epithelial microscopy shows immotile cilia.
lead: Which molecular function is most likely defective?
correct: Dynein-driven force generation for ciliary movement
distractor_notes: CFTR-mediated chloride transport does not explain the directly observed immotile cilia together with a laterality abnormality.
Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase activity does not explain the directly observed defect in motile cilia.
Type IV collagen assembly does not explain the directly observed defect in motile cilia and left-right patterning.
Surfactant phospholipid synthesis does not explain the chronic ciliary-motility phenotype with situs inversus.
key_expl: Axonemal dynein generates the force required for cilia to bend; defective dynein-related proteins can cause PCD with impaired airway clearance and laterality abnormalities.
objective: Explain PCD through defective dynein-dependent ciliary motility.

sources.title: Primary ciliary dyskinesia
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes chronic respiratory infection, laterality abnormalities, infertility, and defective ciliary motion from variants in ciliary genes.

sources.title: DNAH5 gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics explains that DNAH5 encodes an axonemal dynein heavy chain whose dynein arms generate the force needed for cilia to bend.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Repeated upper-airway blockage during sleep reduces or completely stops airflow and can prevent the body from getting enough oxygen.
vignette: A 52-year-old man with obesity has loud snoring, witnessed apneas, morning headaches, and severe daytime sleepiness. A sleep study confirms recurrent breathing pauses during sleep.
lead: Which mechanism best explains these episodes?
correct: Repeated collapse or blockage of the upper airway during sleep
distractors: Transient absence of brainstem respiratory drive with an open airway
Primary failure of diaphragmatic neuromuscular transmission
Loss of surfactant causing global alveolar collapse
distractor_notes: Absent central respiratory drive describes central sleep apnea rather than obstructive apnea with ongoing effort.
Pulmonary thrombosis does not cause repetitive sleep-specific airway obstruction.
Neuromuscular transmission failure causes ventilatory weakness rather than recurrent pharyngeal collapse.
Surfactant failure is not the mechanism of adult OSA.
key_expl: OSA occurs when the upper airway repeatedly narrows or collapses during sleep while breathing effort continues.
objective: Differentiate obstructive sleep apnea from central sleep apnea by upper-airway blockage versus failure of central breathing signals.
clues: obesity with loud snoring and witnessed apneas

sources.title: Sleep Apnea - What Is Sleep Apnea?
sources.support: NHLBI states that OSA occurs when the upper airway becomes blocked repeatedly during sleep and airflow is reduced or stopped.

sources.title: Obstructive sleep apnea - adults
sources.support: MedlinePlus explains that narrowed or blocked upper airways cause sleep-related breathing pauses and loud snoring.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Inhaled respirable crystalline silica causes chronic pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis; chronic disease classically follows years of occupational exposure and also increases tuberculosis risk.
vignette: A 61-year-old stone-cutter has progressive exertional dyspnea and chronic cough after decades of dusty stone work. Imaging shows chronic fibrotic lung disease.
lead: Which exposure most likely caused this disease?
distractor_notes: Asbestos fibers are a different occupational exposure and do not match the documented stone-cutting exposure to respirable crystalline silica.
Coal dust is a different occupational exposure and does not match the documented stone-cutting exposure to respirable crystalline silica.
Beryllium is a different occupational exposure and does not match the documented stone-cutting exposure to respirable crystalline silica.
Cotton dust is a different occupational exposure and does not match the documented stone-cutting exposure to respirable crystalline silica.
key_expl: Silicosis is an occupational fibrotic lung disease caused by inhaling respirable crystalline silica.
objective: Recognize silicosis from long-term silica exposure and chronic fibrotic lung disease.
clues: decades of stone cutting with airborne dust

sources.title: Silica and Worker Health
sources.support: NIOSH states that inhaling excessive respirable crystalline silica causes silicosis and other serious disease.

sources.title: Symptoms and Medical Monitoring - Silica
sources.support: NIOSH describes silica-induced pulmonary inflammation/scarring and increased tuberculosis risk among exposed workers.

outline: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
mechanism: Excess antidiuretic hormone causes the kidneys to retain too much water, diluting blood sodium while urine remains abnormally concentrated.
vignette: A 70-year-old man with a lung mass develops confusion. Serum sodium is 118 mEq/L, his urine is very concentrated, and examination shows normal fluid volume.
lead: Which mechanism most directly causes the hyponatremia?
correct: Excess renal water reabsorption driven by antidiuretic hormone
distractors: Primary renal sodium retention exceeding water retention
Complete absence of antidiuretic hormone secretion
distractor_notes: Preferential sodium retention does not match the excess-water state that dilutes sodium in SIADH.
Complete absence of antidiuretic hormone is the opposite of the excess-ADH state supported by the vignette.
Excessive free-water loss is the opposite of the renal water retention that characterizes SIADH.
Osmotic water loss does not match the excess renal water retention that characterizes SIADH.
key_expl: SIADH causes excess ADH-mediated water retention; the retained water dilutes serum sodium while urine remains concentrated.
objective: Explain SIADH-associated hyponatremia through inappropriate renal water retention.
clues: marked hyponatremia with normal fluid volume
very concentrated urine in a patient with a lung mass

sources.title: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
sources.support: MedlinePlus states that excess ADH makes the kidneys retain too much water and typically produces hyponatremia.

sources.title: Low blood sodium
sources.support: MedlinePlus lists SIADH as a cause of hyponatremia due to inappropriate water retention.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Bacteria enter the bladder and multiply, producing burning urination, urinary frequency or urgency, and lower abdominal discomfort; spread to the kidneys produces a different upper-tract symptom pattern.
vignette: A 24-year-old woman has 2 days of dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort. She is afebrile and has no flank pain or costovertebral-angle tenderness.
distractor_notes: Acute pyelonephritis is less consistent because NIDDK lists fever/chills and back, side, or groin pain as kidney-infection symptoms, which are absent here.
Ureteral nephrolithiasis does not match the verified bacterial bladder-infection symptom cluster presented in this vignette.
Vaginitis does not match the verified bacterial bladder-infection symptom cluster presented in this vignette.
Glomerulonephritis does not match the verified bacterial bladder-infection symptom cluster presented in this vignette.
key_expl: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort without fever or flank pain are characteristic of bladder infection (cystitis).
objective: Differentiate acute cystitis from pyelonephritis and non-bladder causes of dysuria.

sources.title: Symptoms & Causes of Bladder Infection in Adults
sources.support: NIDDK describes burning urination, urinary frequency/urgency, lower abdominal discomfort, and bacteria as the usual cause of bladder infection.

sources.title: Definition & Facts of Bladder Infection in Adults
sources.support: NIDDK defines cystitis/bladder infection as bacterial growth in the bladder and distinguishes complications such as spread to the kidneys.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: An incompetent ureterovesical junction permits urine to flow backward from the bladder into the ureter and sometimes kidney, predisposing children to recurrent febrile UTIs and renal injury.
vignette: A 2-year-old girl has recurrent febrile urinary tract infections. Voiding cystourethrography shows contrast moving from the bladder backward into the left ureter and renal pelvis during urination.
lead: Which defect most directly causes primary vesicoureteral reflux in this child?
correct: Failure of the ureterovesical junction to prevent retrograde urine flow
distractors: A fixed blockage where the ureter joins the renal pelvis
Obstructing folds of tissue within the urethra
A blockage or narrowing at the bladder neck or urethra causing secondary reflux
Abnormal bladder nerve function causing secondary reflux
distractor_notes: A blockage where the ureter joins the renal pelvis is UPJ obstruction, an obstructive lesion rather than primary bladder-to-ureter reflux.
Obstructing urethral folds are posterior urethral valves; NIDDK notes that these cause lower urinary-tract obstruction and occur only in males.
Bladder-neck or urethral obstruction can cause secondary VUR, but the question asks for the defect underlying primary VUR.
Abnormal bladder nerve function can cause secondary VUR, but the question asks for the defect underlying primary VUR.
key_expl: In primary VUR, the valve between the ureter and bladder does not close well, allowing urine to flow backward from the bladder toward the ureter and kidney.
objective: Differentiate primary VUR from obstructive and secondary causes of retrograde urinary flow.
clues: contrast refluxes from bladder to ureter/kidney

sources.title: Vesicoureteral Reflux (VUR)
sources.support: NIDDK defines VUR as backward urine flow from bladder into ureters/kidneys and explains primary VUR from a ureter-bladder valve that does not close well.

sources.title: Hydronephrosis in Newborns
sources.support: NIDDK identifies VUR as a congenital urinary-tract cause of hydronephrosis and urinary infection risk.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: A congenital blockage where the renal pelvis joins the ureter impedes urine drainage and causes upstream hydronephrosis.
vignette: Prenatal ultrasound shows unilateral hydronephrosis. Postnatal imaging demonstrates a dilated renal pelvis with obstruction where the ureter joins the renal pelvis; the bladder and distal ureter are normal.
distractors: Obstruction where the ureter enters the bladder
Transient developmental hydronephrosis without a persistent fixed lesion
distractor_notes: VUR causes backward urine flow from the bladder toward the ureter/kidney rather than the fixed blockage at the renal pelvis–ureter junction shown here.
Posterior urethral valves are a lower urinary-tract obstruction in the urethra and occur only in males.
A distal obstruction where the ureter enters the bladder is anatomically different from the demonstrated blockage where the ureter joins the renal pelvis.
Transient hydronephrosis can resolve as the urinary tract matures and does not match the persistent, localized UPJ-level obstruction described here.
key_expl: UPJ obstruction is a congenital blockage where the ureter joins the renal pelvis and causes hydronephrosis upstream.
objective: Recognize UPJ obstruction as a common congenital obstructive cause of neonatal hydronephrosis.

sources.title: Hydronephrosis in Newborns
sources.support: NIDDK describes UPJ obstruction as a birth defect with blockage where the ureter joins the renal pelvis and identifies it as a cause of hydronephrosis.

sources.title: Vesicoureteral Reflux (VUR)
sources.support: NIDDK distinguishes reflux of urine from obstructive urinary-tract causes and provides the contrasting mechanism.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Struvite stones can form after urinary tract infection and may enlarge rapidly.
vignette: A 48-year-old woman has recurrent urinary tract infections and flank pain. Serial imaging shows a renal stone that has become large over a relatively short interval.
lead: Which type of kidney stone is most likely?
distractor_notes: Calcium oxalate is a common calcium-stone type, but the recurrent-UTI association and rapid enlargement point instead to struvite.
NIDDK notes that uric acid stones may form when urine contains too much acid; that mechanism is not the pattern presented here.
NIDDK states that cystine stones result from inherited cystinuria, which is not the pattern presented here.
Calcium phosphate is a calcium-stone type and does not match the specific recurrent-UTI/rapid-growth pattern NIDDK describes for struvite.
key_expl: NIDDK states that struvite stones may form after a urinary tract infection and can become large quickly.
objective: Recognize struvite nephrolithiasis from its association with urinary tract infection and rapid stone enlargement.

sources.title: Definition & Facts for Kidney Stones
sources.support: NIDDK states that struvite stones may form after a UTI and can become large quickly.

sources.title: Treatment for Kidney Stones
sources.support: NIDDK lists antibiotics and infection-focused therapy for struvite stones, reflecting their infection association.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Uric acid precipitates more readily in persistently acidic urine; excessive urinary uric acid and low urine pH promote uric-acid stone formation.
vignette: A 55-year-old man with gout has recurrent kidney stones. Urinalysis repeatedly shows unusually acidic urine, and stone analysis reveals uric acid.
lead: Which urinary condition most directly promotes formation of this stone?
distractor_notes: NIDDK associates recurrent urinary tract infection with struvite stones rather than the uric acid stone identified here.
NIDDK states that cystinuria causes cystine to enter the urine and produces cystine stones, not uric acid stones.
NIDDK identifies hypercalciuria as a common condition in people who form calcium stones, not the uric acid stone identified here.
NIDDK notes that hyperparathyroidism raises calcium and can promote calcium stones, not the uric acid stone identified here.
key_expl: NIDDK notes that uric-acid stones may form when urine contains too much acid; low urine pH promotes uric-acid precipitation.
objective: Explain why acidic urine predisposes to uric-acid nephrolithiasis.

sources.title: Definition & Facts for Kidney Stones
sources.support: NIDDK states that uric-acid stones may form when urine contains too much acid and describes hyperuricosuria as a risk factor.

sources.title: Treatment for Kidney Stones
sources.support: NIDDK lists potassium citrate, which raises urine pH, as treatment for uric-acid stones.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Long-term heavy use of certain analgesics can cause chronic tubulointerstitial injury and renal papillary necrosis.
vignette: A 59-year-old woman with chronic headaches has taken large amounts of combination over-the-counter analgesics daily for years. She develops slowly progressive kidney dysfunction, and imaging shows renal papillary necrosis.
lead: Which exposure most likely caused her kidney disease?
distractors: Occasional acetaminophen use at recommended doses
distractor_notes: A short medication exposure does not match the years of heavy analgesic overuse that defines the exposure pattern in this vignette.
Occasional acetaminophen use at recommended doses does not match the long-term analgesic overexposure associated with analgesic nephropathy.
A single contrast exposure does not match the chronic analgesic overexposure pattern described here.
Brief dehydration does not match the chronic analgesic overexposure pattern described here.
key_expl: Chronic excessive analgesic exposure can damage renal internal structures and produce interstitial nephritis and papillary necrosis.
objective: Recognize analgesic nephropathy as chronic tubulointerstitial/papillary injury from prolonged heavy analgesic use.
clues: years of heavy combination OTC analgesic use
chronic kidney dysfunction with renal papillary necrosis

sources.title: Analgesic nephropathy
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes kidney damage from long-term overuse of analgesics and notes interstitial nephritis and renal papillary necrosis.

sources.title: Keeping Kidneys Safe: Smart Choices about Medicines
sources.support: NIDDK warns that NSAID pain relievers can damage the kidneys when taken for a long time and specifically discusses over-the-counter pain medicines.
